newsitem.title: CHINA: WTO chief urges China urgency in entry talks.
newsitem.headline: WTO chief urges China urgency in entry talks.

text.p: World Trade Organisation (WTO) Director General Renato Ruggiero urged Chinese leaders on Monday to inject a sense of urgency into their tortuous negotiations to win entry to the global trade body.

"I really hope to give the sense that we have not to lose momentum and we are really waiting for a new and big credible proposal of China," Ruggiero told Reuters before beginning his first full day of talks in Beijing.

Citing the progress achieved in bilateral talks in Geneva last March, Ruggiero urged Chinese Vice Premier Li Lanqing and Minister of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation Wu Yi to ensure Beijing moved faster to ensure its admission.
"Now we have to build on that momentum with a sense of urgency in order to accelerate these negotiations," Ruggiero's spokesman Keith Rockwell quoted him as saying in his talks.

Speaking earlier at Beijing University, Ruggiero described China's entry as a turning point in its relations with the world and stressed both the importance of China's accession and the need for "creative flexibility" in its bid.
"China is too large and important an economic player... to compromise these negotiations," he said.

"China's entry into the global trading system is about more than trade," he said. "It is about China's future role as a world economic leader. And it is about the future direction of the global economy and global community."

Diplomats from countries involved in China's crucial bilateral talks on WTO entry said they had seen little change in recent weeks in China's position on fundamental issues holding up its application for admission, despite the progress in March.

However, Ruggiero, who is not involved in China's entry negotiations since these take place in bilateral talks and with members en bloc, focused on a need for progress on market access -- particularly agriculture and services, Rockwell said.
"We must get from China a credible and good proposal on market access as, of course, we have to make new progress on the protocol," Ruggiero said before his meetings.

Chinese officials acknowledged a need for more flexibility, but stressed there should be a transition with the WTO taking into account the current status of China's economic development -- and not future projections, said sources close to the talks.

Beijing's next opportunity to lay a new offer on the table will come in late May, when non-discrimination -- creating a level playing field -- and ensuring an independent body for judicial review will be among the hottest topics.
Chinese and Western negotiators said last month they had made progress on Beijing's 10-year-old application for membership of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and its successor, the WTO.
However, a wide array of barriers remain to be tackled, diplomats said.

Issues on which bilateral agreement remained distant ranged from opening of China's agriculture markets, financial services, trading rights and distribution systems to clarifying controversial subsidies to state industry, they said.
Diplomats warned that if China did not win entry soon it could find itself without a voice as the WTO makes the rules for trade into the next century.
"If they gain entry only after the rules are made then they will have to abide by rules in whose creation they have had no say," said one Western diplomat.
